slides.title: Sleep can occupy one hemisphere at a time
body: **Unihemispheric slow-wave sleep** is a state in which one cerebral hemisphere expresses the large, slow electrical fluctuations associated with sleep while the other expresses low-amplitude activity resembling wakefulness. The **cerebral hemispheres** are the left and right divisions of the forebrain. Their states can differ within the same animal at the same moment.

Mukhametov and colleagues recorded electrical activity from both sides of the dolphin brain during extended observations in a tank. Slow waves appeared on one side while the opposite side retained a desynchronized pattern. Later, the side expressing slow waves could change.

The sleeping dolphin was often quiet and nearly motionless apart from movements of its fins and flukes. Hemispheric electrical state and overt movement therefore supplied different information: an inactive body could accompany two different patterns of brain activity.

slides.title: Bilateral EEG separates sleep from eye closure
body: An **electroencephalogram**, or EEG, measures voltage differences generated by populations of neurons near recording electrodes. Recording both hemispheres allows researchers to distinguish bilateral sleep from an asymmetric state. Observing only one eye supplies behavioral information without measuring the electrical state of both sides of the brain.

In mallards, simultaneous EEG and eye recordings linked unilateral eye closure to greater slow-wave activity in the opposite hemisphere. Closure of both eyes accompanied bilateral slow-wave sleep or **rapid eye movement sleep**, a sleep state with wake-like electrical activity and characteristic eye movements.

The EEG pattern supplies the neural classification, while the eye recording specifies which visual channel remains available. In _Octopus laqueus_, active sleep includes rapid skin-pattern changes and body movements, yet the animals have increased arousal thresholds, meaning stronger stimulation is required to awaken them. Similar movements during waking therefore require behavioral controls rather than classification by motion alone.

slides.title: Slow-wave power describes local cortical state
body: **Slow-wave activity**, or SWA, is the amount of EEG signal power within a low-frequency band. In the fur-seal study, the band was 1.2–4.0 Hz, meaning approximately one to four oscillations each second. More power in this band indicates stronger slow fluctuations at the recording site.

Electrodes sampled several positions across each **cerebral cortex**, the outer gray-matter tissue of the cerebral hemispheres. During asymmetric sleep, left and right recordings differed across a broad area, but the size of the difference depended on the position of the electrodes.

Posterior and lateral sites often expressed greater asymmetry than medial frontal sites. A hemisphere therefore contains regional variation within its overall sleep state. Comparing matched positions on the two sides separates this anatomical variation from the difference between hemispheres.

slides.title: Open eyes provide intermittent visual monitoring
body: **Contralateral** means on the opposite side; **ipsilateral** means on the same side. During fur-seal unihemispheric sleep, the eye opposite the hemisphere with greater slow-wave activity was almost continuously closed. The opposite eye opened intermittently while its associated hemisphere retained a more activated electrical pattern.

The investigators recorded seals resting at the water surface in a prone posture that allowed both eyes to remain visible. The eye associated with the activated hemisphere opened for about 1.9 s at a time, approximately eight times per minute. It was open during about one quarter of the unihemispheric-sleep period.

Visual vigilance was therefore intermittent rather than a continuously open-eye state. Short openings repeatedly restored access to the surrounding environment while the other eye stayed closed. Eye behavior and bilateral EEG together linked sensory sampling to hemispheric state.

slides.title: Dolphin white-matter pathways are asymmetric
body: **White matter** contains axons that connect neural populations, many wrapped in insulating myelin. **Diffusion tensor imaging** measures directional differences in water diffusion within brain tissue. **Tractography** uses those differences to estimate bundles of pathways through the brain.

Wright and colleagues reconstructed white-matter pathways in a bottlenose dolphin brain. Many bundles had larger estimated volumes on the left, whereas the **arcuate fasciculus**, an association pathway linking regions within a hemisphere, had a rightward bias. Different pathways therefore had different structural asymmetries.

These reconstructions describe the organization through which signals can travel. Structural lateralization and alternating sleep are different biological properties: a permanent left–right difference in a pathway can coexist with a sleep state that changes sides over time.

slides.title: Commissures link the cerebral hemispheres
body: A **commissure** is a bundle of axons crossing between the two sides of the nervous system. The **corpus callosum** connects cerebral regions across the midline, and dolphin tractography reconstructed this pathway within the brain.

The corpus callosum is relatively small in cetaceans compared with their large cerebral hemispheres. Reduced crossing connectivity has been proposed to facilitate hemispheric independence. This is a structural hypothesis about communication between neural populations, rather than a directly measured switch for sleep.

Each hemisphere also contains association pathways linking regions on the same side. Neural organization consequently includes both within-side integration and between-side communication. Unihemispheric sleep occurs in a connected brain whose two sides can express different electrical states.

slides.title: Porpoises retain familiar sleep-regulating nuclei
body: A **nucleus** is an anatomically identifiable group of neurons within the brain. Dell and colleagues mapped neurotransmitter-associated nuclei in the harbor porpoise, an **odontocete**, or toothed cetacean. The main systems also occur in mammals whose hemispheres usually sleep together.

**Immunohistochemistry** uses antibodies to detect particular proteins in tissue. Transmitter-associated markers identified cholinergic, noradrenergic, and serotonergic populations. Calcium-binding proteins supplied indirect markers of neurons associated with **GABA**, gamma-aminobutyric acid, an inhibitory transmitter. Their positions could be related to a series of coronal sections, slices running across the brain from side to side.

No novel sleep nucleus was required to describe the porpoise organization. Differences concerned the size, distribution, and connections of familiar systems. Comparative neuroanatomy therefore places unusual sleep behavior within a recognizable mammalian organization of state-regulating neurons.

slides.title: Basal-forebrain neurons supply acetylcholine
body: The **basal forebrain** contains groups of neurons near the ventral front of the brain that participate in cortical state regulation. **Acetylcholine** is a neurotransmitter released by cholinergic neurons. Antibodies against **choline acetyltransferase**, the enzyme that synthesizes acetylcholine, identified these cells in the porpoise.

Cholinergic neurons occurred in the medial septal and diagonal-band regions, recognizable subdivisions of the basal forebrain. Their organization resembled the corresponding system in other mammals. This anatomy provides a comparative foundation for studying cortical acetylcholine release in fur seals.

Chemical identity and release are complementary measurements. Tissue staining locates cells equipped to synthesize a transmitter; microdialysis during natural behavior measures extracellular transmitter near a probe. Together, the porpoise anatomy and seal physiology connect neuronal organization to state-dependent cortical chemistry.

slides.title: Brainstem transmitter systems remain distributed
body: The **brainstem** connects the forebrain with the spinal cord and contains several state-regulating neuronal groups. The porpoise **locus coeruleus complex** contained neurons marked by **tyrosine hydroxylase**, an enzyme involved in catecholamine synthesis. These populations correspond to noradrenergic systems in other mammals.

**Noradrenaline**, also called norepinephrine, is a transmitter associated with arousal and behavioral activation. Serotonin-positive neurons occupied the **raphe nuclei**, a collection of midline brainstem groups. These populations supply another distributed transmitter system associated with sleep and waking.

The porpoise possessed familiar transmitter systems, with an unusually large noradrenergic population relative to several comparison mammals. Different locus-coeruleus subdivisions varied in cell density and position. Structural differences in these familiar populations supply candidate mechanisms for state regulation, while physiological recordings identify the transmitter changes expressed during an actual sleep episode.

slides.title: Orexin neurons occupy the lateral hypothalamus
body: The **hypothalamus** is a forebrain region involved in coordinating physiological and behavioral states. **Orexin**, also called hypocretin, is a neuropeptide, a transmitter made from a short chain of amino acids. Porpoise orexin-positive neurons occupied the lateral hypothalamic region.

Immunohistochemical staining identified orexin-containing cell bodies and their processes. The **perifornical** group lies near the fornix, a prominent white-matter pathway; additional cells extend laterally. This spatial organization resembles that of orexin populations in other mammals.

Orexin belongs to the wider network associated with arousal. The porpoise and giraffe possessed both larger magnocellular and smaller parvocellular orexin-positive neurons. The porpoise findings complement cortical transmitter measurements in seals: the anatomical map identifies a candidate state-regulating population, while physiological recordings distinguish the chemical changes accompanying particular sleep states.

slides.title: Dolphin hemispheres alternate their EEG states
body: The dolphin recordings contained extended periods of low-amplitude activity in both hemispheres, interspersed with slow waves expressed predominantly on one side. An **electrocorticogram**, or ECoG, is an electrical recording made at or near the cortical surface. Simultaneous left and right ECoG traces resolved this changing relationship.

The investigators classified short epochs according to the amount and amplitude of slow activity. Strong delta activity could occupy one hemisphere while the other retained a waking-like pattern. Across a long recording, the side expressing the stronger slow waves changed repeatedly.

The alternation separated hemispheric state from a permanent anatomical preference for one side. Different cortical recording sites could also begin or end synchronized activity at different times. Sleep organization therefore varied both across the midline and among locations within one hemisphere.

slides.title: Echolocation supports prolonged vigilant behavior
body: **Echolocation** is active sensing in which an animal emits sound and uses returning echoes to investigate objects. Dolphins produce brief clicks and listen for echoes. Branstetter and colleagues coupled each animal’s clicks to underwater electronic targets that simulated returning echoes from particular locations.

Eight projector–receiver stations surrounded an experimental enclosure. A target echo prompted the dolphin to report detection by touching a response paddle. The task required repeated acoustic interrogation, detection of a target among stations, and a learned motor response.

Dolphins maintained this behavior during multi-day sessions. One animal completed a 15-day session with near-perfect target detection. Sustained performance linked active acoustic sampling to repeated responses over a duration far longer than a conventional short attention test.

slides.title: Detection performance and sleep are separate measures
body: A **vigilance task** measures the ability to detect relevant events over time. In the dolphin experiment, successful paddle responses established that the animal continued to use click-dependent target information. They did not identify which hemisphere was asleep at the moment of a response, because the experiment contained no simultaneous EEG.

The animal maintained high detection performance across the 15-day session without a progressive decline. Target accuracy, false alarms, and response latency described different aspects of performance: finding the target, avoiding inappropriate responses, and completing the response promptly.

Behavior also changes with developmental context. In a separate orca study, a four-week-old calf continued circling and vocalizing while its mother began to resume rest behavior. That recording measures overt activity rather than simultaneous EEG. Visible movement, successful target detection, and hemispheric sleep require different measurements.

slides.title: Fur seals change sleep organization between habitats
body: Northern fur seals are **semiaquatic mammals**, animals that use both land and water. On land they express bilateral slow-wave sleep and REM sleep. In seawater, their sleep shifts toward a pronounced left–right difference in slow-wave activity while the body remains at the surface.

The aquatic sleeping posture often raises the head and several flippers above the water. One flipper supplies movements that maintain the posture. The study recorded EEG, muscle activity, and behavior as the same animals moved between land-based and seawater conditions.

Environmental context therefore changes the organization of sleep within one species. A fur seal is neither obligatorily bilateral like a typical terrestrial sleeper nor obligatorily unihemispheric like the classic dolphin pattern. Its natural range of states connects habitat demands with reversible changes in brain and body activity.

slides.title: Aquatic sleep links eye state to EEG asymmetry
body: Fur seals resting prone at the water surface provided simultaneous visibility of both eyes. During right-hemisphere slow-wave sleep, the left eye remained closed while the right eye opened intermittently. When the sleeping side changed, the eye relationship changed with it.

The researchers matched second-by-second eye observations to bilateral EEG power. Slow-wave activity was calculated relative to quiet waking for each hemisphere, allowing comparisons with that hemisphere’s own waking baseline. The stronger-slow-wave side and the eye opposite it changed together across the record.

The association was expressed within natural bouts of rest rather than inferred from isolated photographs. Quiet waking, unihemispheric sleep, and brief REM episodes occupied different portions of the record. Coordinated eye and EEG changes identified how visual access varied as the neural state changed.

slides.title: Sleep asymmetry differs across cortical sites
body: The fur-seal cortex expressed different slow-wave intensities at different anatomical positions. **Parietal** sites lie over the upper and posterior portion of the cerebral cortex; **occipital** sites lie farther toward the rear. These posterior regions often had stronger slow-wave activity than frontal regions during asymmetric sleep.

Bilateral electrode pairs sampled corresponding positions on each side. Comparing the pairs revealed a broadly distributed asymmetry rather than a difference confined to one small visual area. The largest differences occurred in occipital-lateral and parietal recordings.

Regional sampling changes the apparent strength of hemispheric specialization. A frontal recording can report a smaller difference than a posterior recording during the same episode. Anatomical location therefore belongs to the definition of what a measured EEG asymmetry represents.

slides.title: Regional activation can occur within a sleeping side
body: **Local activation** refers to a wake-like electrical pattern restricted to part of an otherwise sleeping brain. Most strongly asymmetric fur-seal episodes combined slow-wave sleep on one side with waking-like activity on the other. A smaller group combined sleep in both hemispheres with activation restricted to a region.

The investigators used multiple electrodes rather than a single left–right pair. This made it possible to identify episodes in which the apparent state depended on the recording site. Approximately nine tenths of asymmetric slow-wave episodes met the study’s unihemispheric classification.

The remaining episodes expanded the range between globally bilateral sleep and a clean hemispheric division. Local cortical regions can differ while neighboring regions remain in a similar state. A hemispheric label captures a dominant pattern, while the full recording preserves the regional organization within it.

slides.title: Acetylcholine tracks the activated hemisphere
body: **Microdialysis** samples extracellular chemicals through a small permeable probe placed in tissue. Lapierre and colleagues measured cortical acetylcholine from both hemispheres while recording fur-seal sleep and waking. The chemical samples were matched to the states expressed during their collection.

Acetylcholine release was lowest during bilateral slow-wave sleep and higher during waking and REM sleep. During asymmetric slow-wave sleep, release was greater on the side with low-voltage, waking-like EEG activity. The opposite side retained lower acetylcholine release together with stronger slow waves.

The chemical difference followed functional state rather than a permanently favored hemisphere. Either side could become the more activated side. The association links cortical acetylcholine to local EEG activation within a single animal whose two hemispheres experience the same surrounding environment.

slides.title: Microdialysis resolves chemical state differences
body: A microdialysis probe contains a membrane through which extracellular molecules enter a flowing sampling solution. The collected fluid is analyzed by **high-performance liquid chromatography**, a separation method that distinguishes chemical compounds before their detection. This supplies a chemical measure alongside the EEG.

The EEG resolves electrical fluctuations over seconds, whereas each chemical sample integrates release over its collection period. The investigators therefore classified the behavior and electrical state present during each sample. Samples dominated by bilateral sleep, waking, or asymmetric sleep could then be compared.

Within asymmetric sleep, acetylcholine release differed between the activated and slow-wave sides. During symmetric states, release changed more similarly in both hemispheres. Separating the time scales of electrical and chemical measurements connects a rapidly changing neural signal to a slower sample of its surrounding chemistry.

slides.title: Serotonin remains similar across the two sides
body: **Serotonin**, also called 5-hydroxytryptamine or 5-HT, is a transmitter produced by brainstem raphe populations. Fur-seal microdialysis measured its extracellular release during natural sleep and waking. Release increased during active waking and was lowest during REM sleep.

During unihemispheric sleep, cortical serotonin did not develop the pronounced lateralization previously measured for acetylcholine. The hemispheres expressed different EEG states while their serotonin measurements remained similar. A waking-like cortical pattern therefore occurred without an accompanying one-sided increase in every arousal-associated transmitter.

Behavioral context also influenced release. Feeding and other activating conditions raised monoamine measurements beyond quieter waking conditions. Serotonin release tracked features of whole-animal activation differently from the local acetylcholine difference between the two cerebral hemispheres.

slides.title: Monoamines differ from lateralized acetylcholine
body: **Monoamines** are a chemical class of transmitters that includes serotonin, noradrenaline, and histamine. **Histamine** participates in arousal-related signaling, while noradrenaline is associated with the locus-coeruleus system. Fur-seal recordings compared all three with previously measured cortical acetylcholine.

Histamine and noradrenaline were higher during active waking and lower during REM sleep. Like serotonin, neither consistently separated into high release on the activated side and low release on the slow-wave side during unihemispheric sleep. Acetylcholine had the distinctive lateralized relationship.

The activated hemisphere consequently combines a waking-like EEG with a transmitter profile that is not simply a miniature copy of whole-animal active waking. Local cortical activation and global behavioral arousal recruit overlapping systems in different ways. The chemical comparison specifies which measured signals covary with hemispheric state.

slides.title: Water suppresses fur-seal REM without a large rebound
body: **Sleep rebound** is an increase in a sleep state after a period in which that state was reduced. Fur seals sharply reduced REM sleep while kept in seawater for days or weeks. The reduction accompanied the shift from bilateral toward asymmetric slow-wave sleep.

After returning to land-based baseline conditions, the seals expressed little or no compensatory REM increase. The accumulated reduction in REM during the water period therefore differed from the large rebound often produced by repeated laboratory awakenings in terrestrial mammals.

The authors proposed a hypothesis that REM helps reverse brain-temperature or metabolic changes associated with bilateral non-REM sleep. The fur-seal result connects habitat-dependent REM reduction with reduced bilateral slow-wave sleep. It places the regulation of REM within the organization of the preceding non-REM state.

slides.title: Elephant seals sleep with both hemispheres at depth
body: Northern elephant seals use a different aquatic strategy from fur seals. Portable EEG recordings detected bilateral slow-wave sleep and REM sleep during deep **drift dives**, dives in which the animal reduces active stroking and descends largely under the influence of buoyancy.

Slow waves appeared in both hemispheres while the seal descended. During REM sleep, low-voltage brain activity accompanied changes in heart rhythm and body orientation. Sleep episodes occurred at depths reaching 377 m in the recorded dives, placing neural sleep within a physically protected underwater interval.

The brain-state recordings anchored later estimates from movement and depth data. A low-activity dive was classified as sleep only after its behavioral pattern had been related to measured EEG. Bilateral diving sleep therefore provides an alternative to maintaining one wake-like hemisphere at the surface.

slides.title: Diving sleep changes posture and movement
body: Elephant seals stopped active swimming during sleep dives and entered descending glides. Bilateral slow-wave sleep often occurred while the animal maintained a stable posture. Transition into REM sleep could bring loss of postural control and an upside-down orientation.

**Sleep spirals** are circular descending trajectories associated with these changes in orientation. EEG, body acceleration, and depth were synchronized to reconstruct the sequence within each dive. The study linked a three-dimensional movement pattern to measured sleep states rather than diagnosing sleep solely from a slow descent.

At sea, modeled sleep averaged about 2 h per day during long foraging migrations, compared with much longer sleep on land. The seals concentrate short sleep opportunities into dives while maintaining extensive daily foraging. Their movement pattern connects the location and timing of rest to oceanic habitat use.

slides.title: Exposed mallards increase asymmetric sleep
body: Mallards sleeping in a row experience different opportunities for detecting an approaching threat. Birds at the ends have an exposed outer side, whereas birds in central positions are flanked by neighbors. Rattenborg and colleagues changed group position while measuring eye state and bilateral EEG.

The proportion of sleep spent unihemispherically rose from about 12% in central positions to about 32% at the edges. Edge birds therefore altered the distribution of sleep states rather than simply remaining awake throughout the rest period. One side continued to express slow waves while the other supplied greater access to visual information.

Group position created a reversible social context for the sleeping animal. The same type of neural state became more common where the environment was less screened by other birds. This links the use of asymmetric sleep to a measurable change in exposure.

slides.title: The open eye faces the exposed environment
body: During unilateral eye closure, an edge mallard could direct its open eye toward its neighbors or away from the group. The outward direction supplied access to the side with no neighboring bird. Central birds had other ducks on both sides and lacked this single exposed direction.

Edge birds oriented the open eye outward during about 86% of unilateral-eye-closure time. Central birds were close to an even split between the two directions. Eye orientation therefore changed together with group position, placing the available visual channel toward the exposed environment.

**Sensory guidance** here concerns which part of the surroundings can supply visual input during sleep. The amount of asymmetric sleep specifies how often one eye is available; head and eye orientation specify where that available channel points. The two behavioral adjustments operate together.

slides.title: Mallards respond to threats during asymmetric sleep
body: An approaching visual stimulus tested whether the open eye could support a behavioral response during unihemispheric sleep. The researchers presented a simulated looming attack while monitoring the duck’s eye state and brain activity. **Looming** is rapid visual expansion associated with an object approaching the observer.

The ducks initiated escape responses with an average latency of approximately 165 ms. The response occurred when the stimulus was presented to the open-eye side. Simultaneous slow-wave activity in the opposite hemisphere preserved the distinction between behavioral detection and a fully bilateral waking state.

Fast escape links sensory access to action while part of the brain remains in a sleeping electrical state. The exposed eye supports a defensive response, and the other hemisphere continues to express slow waves. Predator vigilance therefore has an observable behavioral consequence in this preparation.

slides.title: Group position changes the mallard sleep strategy
body: Unilateral eye closure and bilateral eye closure partition a resting mallard’s sleep behavior. Edge birds spent more time with one eye closed and less time with both eyes closed than centrally positioned birds. Bilateral EEG identified the neural states associated with these eye patterns.

The change was not explained simply by increasing REM sleep, which occurred with both eyes closed. Edge position favored the asymmetric slow-wave pattern that retained an available visual channel. The animal adjusted the type of sleep expressed under different social exposure conditions.

This flexibility differs from a fixed left-eye or right-eye preference. A change in position changes which side faces away from the group, and the sleeping bird can redirect its available eye accordingly. The organization of vigilance follows the surrounding arrangement rather than a permanently selected hemisphere.

slides.title: Unilateral visual experience changes pigeon sleep
body: **Sleep homeostasis** is the regulation of sleep according to prior waking and sleep history. Lesku and colleagues kept pigeons awake for 8 h while they watched a moving video through one eye. The other eye was covered, creating unequal visual input while both sides shared the same prolonged waking period.

The **hyperpallium**, a dorsal avian forebrain region receiving visual information, showed stronger subsequent slow-wave activity on the side associated with the stimulated eye. The sleep response therefore depended on the history of input to a particular neural region, not only on whole-animal time awake.

The **mesopallium**, another pallial region sampled in the experiment, showed a more symmetric recovery response. Local visual activation and overall waking duration consequently produced different spatial patterns. Prior brain use changed where subsequent sleep was most intense.

slides.title: Sleep pressure favors more symmetric bird sleep
body: **Sleep pressure** is the tendency toward sleep that grows with extended waking. High-density EEG in European jackdaws sampled many sites across the dorsal forebrain. Recordings compared ordinary nights with nights following 4 h or 8 h of sleep deprivation.

More intense sleep was accompanied by more similar activity across the two hemispheres.

As the night progressed, asymmetric sleep became more prominent. The opportunity to retain a relatively activated side therefore changed with the history of sleep loss and recovery. Vigilance-related asymmetry competes with the tendency for both sides to express deeper sleep after prolonged waking.

slides.title: Frigatebirds can sleep while remaining airborne
body: Great frigatebirds can remain over the ocean for many days. A head-mounted logger recorded bilateral EEG and acceleration while GPS recorded location and altitude. Electrodes sampled the hyperpallium, enabling electrical-state measurements during natural flight rather than after landing.

The typical flight pattern combined circular rising in thermals with straighter descending glides. **Thermals** are rising air currents that supply lift. Slow-wave sleep occurred mainly during non-flapping flight, when the EEG changed from low-amplitude waking activity to sustained slow waves.

The slow waves were absent during much larger flapping movements and were not coupled to small head movements. This comparison separated neural sleep activity from motion-related recording artifacts. The birds could remain aloft while the brain expressed a recognizable sleeping pattern.

slides.title: Flight EEG resolves unilateral and bilateral sleep
body: Frigatebirds expressed both asymmetric and bilateral slow-wave sleep during flight. **Bilateral slow-wave sleep** means that both recorded hemispheres contain sustained slow waves at the same time. Flight therefore continued even when neither recorded side retained the ordinary waking EEG pattern.

Simultaneous acceleration measurements identified flapping, gliding, and head movement. These measurements were synchronized with left and right EEG, connecting electrical state to the ongoing flight mode. Slow-wave episodes were embedded within a longer record dominated by waking.

The bilateral episodes change the interpretation of aerial sleep. Maintaining flight does not always require one hemisphere to remain electrically wake-like. Aerodynamic support and ongoing movement can continue through neural states that differ from the states expressed during active searching and foraging.

slides.title: Turning direction accompanies EEG asymmetry
body: Circling flight produced sideways acceleration measured by the head-mounted logger. During asymmetric slow-wave sleep, the hemisphere on the side toward which the bird turned tended to express greater slow-wave activity. The pattern reversed when circling direction reversed.

The eye opposite the more activated hemisphere would face into the turn under the usual avian crossing relationship between eye and hemisphere. The authors proposed the hypothesis that this arrangement could help monitor the flight path and other birds within a circling air current. Direct gaze during flight was not measured.

The relationship couples neural lateralization to an ongoing directional behavior rather than assigning one hemisphere a fixed aerial role. Left and right turns occurred with corresponding differences in electrical state. Flight geometry therefore provides a changing behavioral reference for hemispheric activation.

slides.title: Airborne sleep is much shorter than sleep on land
body: Frigatebirds slept for about 0.69 h per day while airborne, approximately 41 min. This was only about 7.4% of the time spent sleeping on land. The birds therefore did not preserve their usual daily sleep duration by distributing a full land-like sleep quota into flight.

Airborne sleep was also shallower, with lower slow-wave intensity than on land. After landing, the birds expressed much more sleep, and the recorded slow-wave pattern changed across the subsequent rest period. **Sleep amount** and **sleep intensity** are separate measurements of this contrast.

The flight record was dominated by waking despite the ability to sleep asymmetrically. The authors interpreted the ecological demand for attention as often exceeding the vigilance available during half-brain sleep. A capacity to sleep while moving does not imply that the animal uses that capacity for most of its journey.

slides.title: Brief REM-like episodes occur during flight
body: Frigatebird slow-wave episodes occasionally shifted into brief activated EEG patterns accompanied by head dropping and twitching. The investigators classified these as apparent REM episodes because the combination resembled REM recorded after the birds returned to land.

slides.title: Bird sleep states extend across pallial regions
body: The **pallium** is the broad forebrain territory containing much of the circuitry for sensory processing and higher integration in birds. Its organization differs from the layered mammalian neocortex. Zebra-finch recordings sampled both surface EEG and signals from deeper pallial sites.

A **local field potential**, or LFP, measures extracellular voltage near an implanted electrode. Yeganegi and Ondracek recorded from the **dorsal ventricular ridge**, a group of deeper pallial structures, as well as the hyperpallium. Each site was scored independently rather than being assigned a state solely from the surface EEG.

Sleep classifications could differ across simultaneously recorded locations. Some deeper sites shared temporal state patterns more closely with one another than with surface recordings. Local differences therefore occurred within the avian forebrain even without an experimental manipulation of preceding visual experience.

slides.title: Songbird regions can enter different sleep states
body: Simultaneous zebra-finch recordings contained intervals in which different pallial sites met different sleep-stage criteria. A surface hyperpallial signal and a deeper dorsal-ventricular-ridge signal could diverge in their slow-wave or activated electrical patterns within the same time interval.

Independent scoring preserved these mismatches. Assigning every site the stage detected at one electrode would instead erase regional differences by definition. The experiment compared the timing of transitions across locations as well as the frequency content of their electrical activity.

The resulting **state congruence**, agreement in sleep classification between sites, varied with anatomical location. Deeper sites had a strong role in the timing of shared states. Brain-wide labels therefore summarize a dominant pattern while local recordings retain transitions and states expressed by particular neural territories.

slides.title: Pigeon REM activates broad brain territories
body: **Functional magnetic resonance imaging**, or fMRI, measures changes in signals associated with blood oxygenation and flow. The **BOLD signal**, blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal, supplies an indirect measure of neural activity. Naturally sleeping pigeons were habituated to head fixation within the scanner.

REM sleep produced widespread increases in BOLD signal relative to NREM sleep, including regions involved in visual processing. Eye and beak observations supported sleep-state classification. The original supplementary recording captures transitions marked by pupil constriction and rapid eye and bill movements.

**Cerebrospinal fluid**, or CSF, surrounds the brain and occupies its ventricles. Ventricular CSF flow increased during NREM relative to waking but dropped during REM. Neural activation and fluid-flow measures consequently changed in different directions across the two sleep states.

slides.title: Crocodiles direct one open eye toward intruders
body: Juvenile saltwater crocodiles sometimes rested with one eye closed and the other open. **Unilateral eye closure** describes this visible behavior without assigning an electrical sleep state. Kelly and colleagues compared ordinary rest with exposure to another crocodile or to a human.

The crocodiles directed the available eye preferentially toward the nearby animal or human. Human presence also increased unilateral-eye-closure behavior, and the effect persisted after the person withdrew. The resting animal changed its sensory orientation according to a stimulus in its surroundings.

This study used behavioral observations without bilateral EEG, so it establishes directed eye use rather than confirmed unihemispheric sleep. The distinction changes the cross-species comparison: crocodiles share a vigilance-related eye pattern with birds and marine mammals, while the neural state underlying that pattern remains a separate measurement.

slides.title: Dogs show smaller NREM hemispheric differences
body: Family dogs slept during afternoon recordings at the same location on two occasions. **Polysomnography** combines measurements such as EEG, eye activity, and muscle signals to classify sleep. Bilateral channels permitted comparison of left and right activity during NREM sleep.

In the first sleep cycle of the first recording, low-frequency activity was stronger on the left. This directional difference was reduced in the corresponding cycle of the second recording. Other frequency ranges changed in the strength of asymmetry between successive sleep cycles.

The dogs’ pattern was a difference within NREM sleep rather than the pronounced sleep-versus-wake division found in dolphins. It also differed from the human first-night pattern in its direction and dynamics. Comparative sleep asymmetry includes several neural organizations rather than one universal half-brain strategy.

The asymmetry was reduced on the second recording night. Unusual sounds also produced stronger left-sided responses on the first night, with more awakenings in trials favoring that side. Standard repeated sounds did not produce the same hemispheric difference in response.

This was a regional difference during sleep rather than an entire waking hemisphere. The authors proposed a **night-watch hypothesis**, in which asymmetric reactivity contributes to environmental monitoring in an unfamiliar setting. Familiarity changed both the slow-wave difference and the response to unusual sensory events.

slides.title: Detection and awakening measure different operations
body: An **auditory oddball** sequence contains common standard sounds interrupted by less frequent deviant sounds. During slow-wave sleep, the human experiment presented these sounds to one ear at a time. Unusual sounds evoked different responses from repeated standards.

First-night awakenings were more common for trials favoring left-hemisphere processing. In a behavioral experiment, participants tapped a finger after awakening to a deviant sound. Faster overall responses on the first night reflected earlier awakening rather than a shorter motor delay after awakening.

The sequence separates several operations: sensory-evoked brain activity, transition out of sleep, and an instructed action after awakening. A response recorded during sleep is therefore distinct from conscious reporting after the sleeper becomes awake. The timing of each measurement determines which operation the experiment identifies.

slides.title: Local sleep changes the meaning of a whole-brain label
body: Unihemispheric sleep divides the dominant electrical state across the cerebral midline. Regional sleep differences can also occur within a hemisphere or between surface and deeper sites. Fur-seal and zebra-finch recordings reveal these spatial differences when several locations are measured simultaneously.

Behavior provides another level of organization. Frigatebirds continue aerodynamic movement during asymmetric and bilateral sleep; mallards respond to looming threats during asymmetric sleep. Octopuses produce similar skin patterns during waking and active sleep. Increased arousal thresholds and sleep homeostasis, the regulation of subsequent sleep by prior sleep loss, distinguish their sleep from waking; these findings concern sleep stages rather than unihemispheric sleep.

**Consciousness** concerns experience, while EEG, transmitter release, eye opening, and task responses are measured physiological or behavioral variables. The studies constrain which processes continue during sleep and where sleep-related activity occurs. They support a spatially distributed account of state without supplying a direct measure of another animal’s subjective experience.

Behavior provides another level of organization. Frigatebirds continue aerodynamic movement during asymmetric and bilateral sleep; mallards respond to looming threats during asymmetric sleep. Octopuses produce similar skin patterns during waking and active sleep. Increased arousal thresholds and sleep homeostasis, the regulation of subsequent sleep by prior sleep loss, distinguish their sleep from waking; these findings concern sleep stages rather than unihemispheric sleep.

Consciousness concerns experience, while EEG, transmitter release, eye opening, and task responses are measured physiological or behavioral variables. The studies constrain which processes continue during sleep and where sleep-related activity occurs. They support a spatially distributed account of state without supplying a direct measure of another animal’s subjective experience.
The boundaries established here are boundaries between measured neural states and retained functions. Claims about subjective experience require evidence beyond the measurements made in these papers.

The paired waking and active-sleep recordings contain similar skin patterns. The paper classified sleep using reversibility, arousal threshold and homeostatic regulation rather than skin appearance alone. Similar patterns do not identify dreams or subjective experiences.

items.text: Unihemispheric slow-wave sleep combines stronger slow waves on one side with waking-like activity on the other. Bilateral EEG distinguishes this state from eye closure alone.
Cetaceans retain familiar cholinergic, monoaminergic, and orexinergic systems. Anatomical differences supply mechanistic hypotheses, while chemical release and EEG measure physiological state.
Fur-seal cortical acetylcholine is lateralized with EEG activation; measured serotonin, noradrenaline, and histamine do not acquire the same consistent hemispheric separation.
Mallards adjust sleep and eye direction to group exposure. Prior visual use changes local pigeon sleep, while higher jackdaw sleep pressure favors more symmetric sleep.
Fur seals favor asymmetric surface sleep, elephant seals sleep bilaterally during deep dives, and frigatebirds express both forms during flight while greatly reducing daily sleep.
Local EEG state, ongoing movement, sensory responses, awakening, and conscious reporting are different measurements. Cross-species comparisons preserve these distinctions.
